items.title: Why are the USA and Iran fighting?
items.headline: Iran strikes at a US air base in Kuwait and at Bahrain, as tankers with Indian crews are hit near Hormuz
items.news: On 17 November 2026, a US fighter jet struck a missile launch site of Iran's Revolutionary Guards on Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, after Iran attacked a US radar in Bahrain earlier that day. Early on 18 November, Iran targeted Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, which US forces use, and launched several attacks on Bahrain, home to the US Navy's 5th Fleet; both countries said their air defences intercepted the attacks. On 16 November, the gas tanker Tara Gas, with 24 Indian sailors on board, was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, in what Indian officials called a missile attack; 21 were taken safely to Khasab in Oman, two went to hospital and one was missing. On 18 November, another tanker, Navig8 Messi, with three Indians on board, was hit near Hormuz, and India's shipping minister said all its crew were safe. India's Ministry of External Affairs called the attacks on ships "deeply worrisome" and asked for them to stop. This entry explains how a quarrel that began more than 70 years ago turned into this war.
items.hook: For about 25 years after 1953, the USA and Iran were close friends. Since 1979 they have been rivals, and in 2026 that rivalry became a war that reached Indian kitchens, airports and ships.

items.title: What makes a great captain?
items.headline: MS Dhoni retires from the IPL and becomes Chennai Super Kings' team mentor
items.news: On Tuesday 17 November 2026, it was announced that MS Dhoni had retired as a player from the Indian Premier League. He will stay with Chennai Super Kings as the team's mentor from the 2027 season. The news came on the day IPL teams had to name the players they were keeping for 2027. Dhoni, now 45, first played for Chennai in the very first IPL season in 2008, captained them to five titles, and did not play in the 2026 season. He retired from international cricket in August 2020. This entry explains the skill his career is most remembered for, leading a team under pressure.
items.hook: A captain cannot bat for everyone or bowl every ball. Yet one quiet decision, like who bowls the last over, can win or lose a World Cup.

items.title: How does a film make money at the box office?
items.headline: Ramayana: Part 1 sells more than 1,200 crore rupees of tickets worldwide in its first ten days
items.news: Ramayana, a big-budget film of the ancient epic directed by Nitesh Tiwari, with Ranbir Kapoor as Ram and Yash as Ravana, opened in cinemas on 5 November 2026, in the week of Diwali. Its makers planned a release on about 59,000 screens around the world. On Monday 9 November, early estimates from the tracking site Sacnilk said it earned more in India than any Indian film had ever earned on a first Monday. By its tenth day, trade trackers estimated it had made more than 1,200 crore rupees worldwide, about 820 crore of it in India and the rest abroad. These are estimates from the film trade, not official figures. This entry explains what those big box office numbers really count, and how much of the money a film's makers actually get.
items.hook: When a headline says a film "made 1,000 crore", that money does not land in one pocket. The government, the cinema and the film's makers all take a piece, and the makers usually get well under half.

items.title: How can a company lose a trillion dollars in a week?
items.headline: Nvidia says Jensen Huang has stepped down as its boss, and finance chief Colette Kress is leading it for now
items.news: On 12 November 2026, Nvidia, the American company whose chips power much of the world's artificial intelligence, said its co-founder Jensen Huang had resigned as chief executive and left its board, with immediate effect, giving no reason. US news reports linked his exit to a board investigation, still unfinished, into reports about his private life and whether a foreign spy had targeted him; The Wall Street Journal had reported that the board was preparing to remove him. Colette Kress, the company's finance chief, now leads Nvidia as interim chief executive while the board looks for a permanent one. News reports said Nvidia was worth about 5.8 trillion dollars at its record in early October, and about 3.9 trillion dollars by 13 November, partly because AI shares were falling everywhere. Nvidia reports its results for the latest three months on 17 November. This entry explains how a company's value can rise and fall so fast.
items.hook: In 2026, the chipmaker Nvidia was worth more than every company on India's stock market put together. Within weeks, more than a trillion dollars of that value vanished, yet the company still had its factories, its chips and its customers.

items.title: Why does the narrow Strait of Hormuz matter so much to the world?
items.headline: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say three oil tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz
items.news: On 14 November 2026, Iran's state news agency IRNA quoted the navy of Iran's Revolutionary Guards as saying three oil tankers caught fire after hitting sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz. It said the ships were trying to use a route Iran has banned. Reuters said it could not check the claim. A day earlier, the Revolutionary Guard said it had struck a US early warning radar in Bahrain. The US military said this was not true. It said it shot down two Iranian drones flying towards Bahrain, and that nothing was damaged and no one was hurt. Far fewer ships than normal have used the strait since the USA and Israel began strikes on Iran on 28 February 2026 and Iran hit back. A barrel of Brent crude cost about 96 dollars in mid-November, against about 73 dollars just before the war. In early November, a senior Iranian lawmaker said ships from India could pass, and that they would pay a fee. This entry explains why one narrow strip of sea can move petrol and gas prices in Indian homes.
items.hook: Between Iran and Oman lies a strip of sea less than 40 km wide. In normal times, about one in every five barrels of oil the world burns sails through it, and so does much of the cooking gas in Indian kitchens.

items.title: What is a tariff?
items.headline: The US promises India lower tariffs than its rivals under a new trade deal
items.news: On 13 November 2026, a senior Indian government official, speaking without giving their name, told Business Standard that the United States had assured India its exporters would get better tariff treatment than competing countries. The official said this would come once the US finished a trade investigation and settled its new tariff rules. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal had said for months that India would put the deal into effect only once it got a tariff edge over rival exporters such as Vietnam, Bangladesh and Indonesia. The exact rates were not made public, and the interim deal had not yet been signed. On the same day, India reported its highest-ever monthly goods exports. This entry explains what a tariff is and why a few percentage points matter so much.
items.hook: When a T-shirt made in Tiruppur is sold in New York, the USA may add a tax at its border before it reaches the shop. That tax, called a tariff, can decide whether the shirt sells or sits on a shelf.

items.title: What is a trade deficit?
items.headline: India's exports hit a record, but its goods trade gap is the widest in a year
items.news: On 13 November 2026, the commerce ministry said India sold goods worth 49.47 billion dollars abroad in October, the highest for any month in its history. But imports jumped to 89.35 billion dollars, as gold imports more than tripled before Diwali and oil cost much more, so the goods trade deficit reached 39.88 billion dollars, the biggest in a year. India also earned a surplus of about 19.8 billion dollars from services like software, which cut the overall gap to about 20 billion dollars. This entry explains what a trade deficit is and when it matters.
items.hook: In October 2026, India sold more goods to the world than in any month in its history. Yet it still bought far more than it sold. How can a country break a record and fall behind at the same time?

items.title: Why does the RBI try to keep inflation near 4%?
items.headline: Price rises cross the RBI's 6% limit for the first time in two years
items.news: On 12 November 2026, the government said retail inflation in October was 6.09%, up from 5.54% in September and the highest in two years. That is above 6%, the top of the safe band the Reserve Bank of India must aim for. Food prices rose 8.94% in a year, and onions cost more than twice as much as a year earlier. The RBI had already raised its main interest rate, the repo rate, by 0.25 percentage points to 5.50% in October, its first rise in nearly four years, and economists expected another rise at its December meeting. This entry explains why the RBI aims for 4% and how it tries to get there.
items.hook: India's central bank has a promise written into law. It must try to keep price rises close to 4% a year, and if it misses for too long, it has to write to the government and explain why.

items.title: Why are Russia and Ukraine at war?
items.headline: Russia and Ukraine sit down for US-led peace talks for the first time since February
items.news: On 10 November 2026, delegations from Russia and Ukraine met in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, for talks run by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. It was their first three-way meeting since February, and the first day lasted about four hours. On the table were land Russia wants Ukraine to give up, Russia's demand that Ukraine drop its bid to join NATO, limits on Ukraine's army, whether a ceasefire should come first, and swaps of prisoners. India called for safe shipping in the Black Sea and a quick end to the war. This entry explains how the war began and what each side wants.
items.hook: Russia and Ukraine share a long history, related languages and many family ties. Yet since 2022 they have fought the biggest war in Europe in 80 years, and its effects reach Indian kitchens and petrol pumps.

items.title: What does the AQI number mean?
items.headline: Delhi's air turned 'severe' on Diwali night
items.news: On Diwali night, 8 November 2026, 20 of Delhi's 59 air monitoring stations showed AQI readings above 400, in the severe band. The city's average for the whole day was 376, which is very poor. Smoke from firecrackers mixed with cold, still winter air that trapped it close to the ground. Down To Earth found that Delhi's air had got worse on the day after Diwali in eight of the past nine years. This entry explains what those AQI numbers mean and how they are worked out.
items.hook: On a smoggy day, the news says the AQI is 400. That one number squeezes a whole cocktail of invisible pollution into something you can read at a glance.

items.title: What happens at a world climate summit?
items.headline: COP31, the world's yearly climate summit, opens in Antalya, Türkiye
items.news: The COP31 climate summit opened on 9 November 2026 in Antalya, Türkiye, and runs until 20 November, with delegates from 197 countries and the European Union. Türkiye is the host, Australia is leading the negotiations, and more than 100 heads of state were expected at a leaders' meeting on 11 and 12 November. India said it would press rich countries for more climate money, and that countries should keep setting their own emission targets instead of having new ones handed down to them. A UN report said poorer countries will need about USD 305 billion a year by 2035 just to adapt to a hotter world. This entry explains how these summits work.
items.hook: Once a year, almost every country on Earth sends people to one city to argue about the weather of the future. Nothing can be agreed unless nearly everyone says yes.

items.title: Why do countries do science together?
items.headline: India set to join Horizon Europe, the EU's €93.5 billion research programme
items.news: On 6 November 2026, India and the European Union finished talks on India joining Horizon Europe, the EU's €93.5 billion programme for research and new ideas. Once both sides sign and approve the deal, expected to take effect in January 2027, Indian universities, labs and companies can win grants directly and lead projects with European partners. The work covers health, artificial intelligence, space, climate and clean energy. India will be one of more than 20 non-EU countries in the programme, alongside the UK, Canada, Japan and South Korea. This entry explains why countries team up on science.
items.hook: Some machines are so big and so costly that no single country can build them alone. So countries that may disagree about almost everything else end up sharing a lab.

items.title: Why do we pay to use some roads?
items.headline: New highways will get toll plazas where cars pay without stopping
items.news: On 6 November 2026, the National Highways Authority of India issued a standard design for toll plazas on four-lane and wider national highways. It sets common rules for plaza layout, lanes, lighting and signs, so every new highway can use barrier-free tolling, called Multi-Lane Free Flow. A FASTag reader and number-plate cameras on an overhead frame collect the toll while cars keep moving. The first such plaza opened at Choryasi in Gujarat on 1 May 2026, and the first six handled about 1.1 crore vehicles in three months. This entry explains why highways charge tolls at all.
items.hook: Most streets are free to drive on. Then, on a big highway, a sign appears asking for money. Why do some roads charge and others don't?

items.title: What are America's midterm elections, and why do they matter?
items.headline: Americans vote in the 2026 midterm elections for the US Congress
items.news: Americans voted on 3 November 2026, choosing all 435 members of the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 senators. News reports, including Reuters, said the Democratic Party had won enough seats to lead both the House and the Senate, which President Donald Trump's Republican Party had led before. In a large survey of voters by the AP news agency, about 7 in 10 said Congress was not doing enough to check the president's power. For the next two years, the president will need the other party's votes to pass laws, which could shape US decisions on tariffs and trade, including with India. This entry explains how midterms work and why they matter so much.
items.hook: Every four years, Americans choose a president. But two years into each term, they vote again, and that vote can decide whether the president gets anything done at all.
